title: What Can Console Me? No Family, No Home
intro: Al-Mutanabbi wrote this in Egypt when word reached him that some people had announced his death in the council of Sayf al-Dawla, his former patron in Aleppo; the commentator al-Wahidi places it in 348 AH (959 CE). It opens with the loneliness of exile and a few lines of hard-won wisdom about the world, then turns on the court he has left: the men who spread news of his death, and a prince and courtiers he paints as fickle and spiteful, their gifts spoiled by reproach. He closes by praising his stay with Kafur, the ruler of Egypt, and explains a delay in Kafur's promised reward as a test of the love the poet has professed. Ibn Jinni heard from the poet himself of a man who quoted the opening line in a letter to his wife, only to be told that he was more like another line of the same poem: sleepless after leaving, and then sleeping again. Al-Sahib ibn Abbad put three of its lines in his collection of al-Mutanabbi's proverbial verse, among them “the winds blow as the ships would not wish”.

translation: What is there to console me? No family, no homeland,
no friend to drink with, no cup, no one to rest with.
1.sharh: Far from his family and his country, he has nothing left to take his mind off his troubles: no drinking companion, no wine, no one to find comfort in. The line is a complaint against fortune.

translation: I want this time of mine to bring me
what time itself cannot reach for itself.
2.sharh: He wants fortune to give him what it cannot even give itself. Ibn Jinni explains that time, if it could choose, would be spring all year and cannot; al-Wahidi, that he asks for steadiness from something made of changing seasons and of night and day.

translation: Face fortune with nothing but indifference
as long as your body keeps your soul company.
3.sharh: As long as you are alive, take whatever fortune does without being shaken by it. Its blows pass, and the one loss that can never be made good is life itself.

translation: The joy of what delights you does not last,
and grief will not bring back what you have lost.
4.sharh: This confirms the line before: joy does not last, because what brings it does not last, and grieving over a loss will not bring it back. Al-Sahib ibn Abbad quotes it as “joy does not make what delights you last”.

translation: Part of what has harmed the lovers is that
they loved before they knew the world or saw through it.
5.sharh: Lovers come to grief because they give their hearts before they learn how faithless the world and its people are. Al-Wahidi took the lovers to be lovers of the world itself; al-Barquqi reads it of every lover.

translation: Their eyes waste away in tears, their souls in grief,
chasing every ugly thing that has a lovely face.
6.sharh: They weep their eyes away and wear their souls out with sorrow, chasing things that look fair and prove foul. Al-Wahidi says he means the world and its pleasures.

translation: Go, then, and may every swift camel carry you off;
today I trust every parting to do me no harm.
7.sharh: He tells the departing loved ones to go, and wishes them fast camels to carry them off: parting holds no fear for him now. Ibn Jinni calls it the love prelude of a man nursing a grievance.

translation: Nothing in your litters would repay my soul
if I died of longing, nor is anything there worth its price.
8.sharh: The women in those litters are not worth dying of longing for; nothing they hold could make up for his life or pay its price.

translation: You, in whose council my death was announced far away:
everyone is held in pledge to what the heralds claimed.
9.sharh: He turns to the prince in whose court his death was announced: the death they claimed for him awaits everyone, the heralds and the prince included.

translation: How often I have been killed, how often I have died among you,
then shaken myself, and grave and shroud were gone.
10.sharh: Reports of his death have reached that court many times and been believed, yet each time he has risen alive, as if shaking off grave and shroud. Al-Ukbari reads it as a dig at Sayf al-Dawla.

translation: Before they said it, a group had witnessed my burial,
and then they died before the one they buried.
11.sharh: Before these heralds, others claimed to have seen him buried, and they died before him. Al-Ma'arri points out the mockery: the men who buried him went first.

translation: A man does not attain all that he wishes for:
the winds blow as the ships would not wish.
12.sharh: Not every wish comes true; the wind often blows against what the sailors want. His enemies wished him dead and did not get their wish. The line became a proverb.

translation: I found that your neighbour cannot guard his honour,
and on your pasture no milk flows.
13.sharh: At their court a neighbour's good name is not safe from them, and their pasture is so bad that grazing animals give no milk. Al-Wahidi counts it among the most painful satire; al-Ma'arri takes the milk for any good that comes from them.

translation: Whoever comes near you is rewarded with weariness;
whoever loves you gets rancour for his share.
14.sharh: They repay closeness with boredom and love with resentment, so that neither those near them nor those who love them get what they deserve. Al-Barquqi reads all these lines as a bitter attack on Sayf al-Dawla.

translation: You grow angry with whoever receives your gifts,
until bitterness and reminders of favour punish him.
15.sharh: Their gifts come with anger and constant reminders, until receiving one is a punishment. Al-Wahidi says all of this is aimed at Sayf al-Dawla. Al-Ma'arri also allows the verb to mean “takes turns with”: the gift and the bitterness never come together, and in the end the bitterness comes alone.

translation: Estrangement has left between you and me
a trackless waste where the eye and the ear lie.
16.sharh: The break between them has become a vast, pathless desert, where travellers see and hear things that are not there. Al-Wahidi reads it as a wish for distance; Ibn Jinni, al-Ma'arri and al-Barquqi as news that he is already far away.

translation: Swift camels crawl there after their racing gait,
and their knees ask the ground where their feet have gone.
17.sharh: The desert is so long that the swiftest camels end up crawling, their pads worn away, as if their knees were asking the earth where their feet had gone. The question is a figure for the hardship of the journey.

translation: I keep my forbearance while it is generosity in me;
I do not keep it when it would be cowardice.
18.sharh: He holds back his anger only while restraint is a mark of generosity; when it would look like fear, he drops it. The commentators compare a half-line of al-Find al-Zimmani: “some forbearance, in the face of insolence, is surrender to humiliation”.

translation: I do not stay for wealth that brings me humiliation,
nor take pleasure in what leaves my honour soiled.
19.sharh: Wealth and pleasure come second to his good name: money that comes with humiliation he leaves behind, and nothing that would soil his honour gives him pleasure, however sweet.

translation: After I left I lay awake, missing you;
then my resolve grew firm and sleep came back.
20.sharh: When he first left them, he could not sleep for missing them; then he steadied himself and sleep returned. In other words, he is over them.

translation: If I am tried with a love like yours,
I am apt to make a parting like this one.
21.sharh: If he meets the same kind of love elsewhere, a love that is not sincere, he will leave that place too. Al-Wahidi sees a warning to Kafur here. Ibn Jinni reports that Sayf al-Dawla, hearing the line, said “By my father, he is on his way.”

translation: My colt has worn out its saddle-cloths with others than you,
its cheek-straps and halter changed for new ones in Fustat,
22.sharh: He has stayed so long in Egypt, and been so well treated, that his horse's coverings have worn out and its bridle and halter have had to be replaced.

translation: with the noble Abu al-Misk, in whose generosity
Mudar of the red and Yemen have drowned.
23.sharh: His host is Kafur, whose generosity, he says, has flooded all the Arabs, north and south. Ibn Jinni thought the praise went too far: “God forbid it should be so.”

translation: And if some of what he promised me is slow in coming,
my hopes do not lag behind, nor do they weaken.
24.sharh: Some of what Kafur promised him has not come yet, but his hopes have neither slowed nor weakened. Al-Barquqi takes the promise to be a governorship; the next line gives the reason for the delay.

translation: He keeps his word, but I told him
of my love, and he is testing it, trying it out.
25.sharh: Kafur keeps his word; he is only testing the love the poet has professed before he rewards it. The delay is a trial, not a broken promise.

1.1.2.head: التَّعَلُّل
1.1.2.meaning: Ta'allul: distracting oneself, finding something to while away a sorrow.

1.2.2.head: نَديم
1.2.2.meaning: Nadim: a drinking companion, a friend for the evening's talk.

1.2.6.head: سَكَن
1.2.6.meaning: Sakan: anyone or anything one finds rest and comfort in, family or a friend.

3.1.6.head: مُكتَرِث
3.1.6.meaning: Caring, troubled; from a root meaning to weigh heavily on someone.

7.1.2.head: حَمَلَ
7.1.2.meaning: “It carried you”: a past-tense verb used as a wish, may it carry you; here a wish to see them gone.

8.1.3.head: هَوادِج
8.1.3.meaning: Howdahs: the covered litters in which women rode on camels.

8.1.5.head: مُهجَة
8.1.5.meaning: Muhja: life, the soul; literally the heart's blood.

9.2.5.head: مُرتَهَن
9.2.5.meaning: Held in pledge: bound to something with no escape, like a pawned thing; here, bound to die.

10.2.2.head: اِنتَفَضَ
10.2.2.meaning: Shook myself, as one shakes off dust.

13.1.4.head: العِرض
13.1.4.meaning: Ird: a man's honour, his good name.

15.2.4.head: المِنَن
15.2.4.meaning: Reminders of favour: a giver's habit of recounting his gifts to the one who received them.

16.2.1.head: يَهماء
16.2.1.meaning: Yahma': a trackless desert, without water or landmarks.

17.1.2.head: الرَّواسِم
17.1.2.meaning: Rawasim: camels that go at the rasim, a fast gait.

17.2.5.head: الثَّفِن
17.2.5.meaning: Thafin: the callused pads, knees and chest, on which a camel kneels.

18.1.3.head: حِلم
18.1.3.meaning: Hilm: forbearance, self-command, the patience to pardon.

19.2.6.head: دَرَن
19.2.6.meaning: Daran: dirt; the noun stands for the adjective, as if his honour became dirt itself. The editions print darin, dirty.

20.2.3.head: مَرير
20.2.3.meaning: Marir: a tightly twisted rope; “my rope grew firm” means his resolve grew strong.

22.1.2.head: الأَجِلَّة
22.1.2.meaning: Saddle-cloths, the coverings put on a horse to protect it.

22.2.3.head: الفُسطاط
22.2.3.meaning: Al-Fustat: the capital of Egypt in the poet's day, a name used for Egypt itself.

23.1.3-4.head: أَبو المِسك
23.1.3-4.meaning: Abu al-Misk: “father of musk”, the byname of Kafur al-Ikhshidi, ruler of Egypt.

23.2.3-4.head: مُضَر الحَمراء
23.2.3-4.meaning: “Mudar of the red”: Mudar ibn Nizar, ancestor of many northern Arab tribes; when Nizar's estate was divided, Mudar is said to have received the gold, or a red tent.

23.2.5.head: اليَمَن
23.2.5.meaning: Yemen: the southern Arab tribes, not descended from Mudar; the two together mean all the Arabs.
